title: Ordaining the Priests and the Daily Offering
summary: God gives Moses a seven-day ceremony to consecrate Aaron and his sons as priests: washing, clothing, anointing, a sin offering, a burnt offering, and a ram of ordination whose blood marks their ears, thumbs, and toes. The altar itself is purified and made most holy. The chapter closes by setting up the regular morning and evening offering of lambs and with God's promise to meet with Israel, dwell among them, and be their God.
story: Chapter 28 described the garments of the priests; this chapter describes how the men who wear them are to be installed. The ceremony will actually be carried out in Leviticus 8, after the tabernacle is built. The instructions for the tabernacle (chapters 25-31) are nearly complete, and this chapter reaches their theological high point in verses 45-46: the whole purpose of the tent, the altar, and the priesthood is that God might live among the people he brought out of Egypt. The exodus was not only an escape from slavery; it was so that God could dwell with his people. That promise will be tested almost immediately, when Israel breaks the covenant with the golden calf in chapter 32, and renewed when God's glory fills the finished tabernacle in chapter 40.
historical:
The setting is the camp at Sinai, and the questions of date and composition noted at chapters 13 and 28 apply here too. Many scholars assign this material to a priestly source and connect it with worship at the Jerusalem temple; others see in it early traditions of Israel's sanctuary. Whatever its history of composition, the rites it describes became part of Israel's settled practice. The daily morning and evening offering (the tamid, meaning regular or continual) was offered at the temple in Jerusalem for centuries, and its interruption was felt as a disaster (Daniel 8:11 speaks of it being taken away). In the New Testament, Luke's Gospel opens with the priest Zechariah serving at the temple at the hour of incense, while the people pray outside (Luke 1:8-10), a scene set within this pattern of daily worship.

Sacrifice was universal in the ancient Near East. Egyptian, Mesopotamian, and Canaanite temples all offered animals, grain, and drink to their gods, and priests were installed with ceremonies. The sacrificial terms in this chapter (burnt offering, sin offering, peace offering, wave offering) are laid out more fully in Leviticus 1-7.
cultural:
The ceremony draws on symbols its first readers understood. Washing signaled cleansing before entering a holy place. Anointing with oil set a person or object apart for a special role; kings and, in some passages, prophets were anointed too, and the Hebrew word for anointed one is the source of the title Messiah. Laying hands on an animal's head identified the offerer with the animal being offered. The “fat tail” in verse 22 belongs to the broad-tailed sheep common in the region, whose tail stores a large amount of fat and was considered a choice portion. The fat of an offering belonged to God and was burned, while specific parts (the breast and thigh) became the priests' share, which is how Israel supported its priests.

The blood placed on the right ear, right thumb, and right big toe is the chapter's most striking gesture. The same marking appears in the cleansing of someone healed of a skin disease (Leviticus 14:14). Interpreters commonly read it as consecrating the whole person, from the ear that hears God's word to the hand that serves and the foot that walks, though the text itself doesn't explain it. The Hebrew idiom for ordination is literally to fill the hand, and in verses 24-25 Moses actually fills the priests' hands with the offerings.
literary: The chapter is written as a sequence of ritual instructions, with each step introduced by a command to Moses: take, present, wash, clothe, anoint, slaughter, sprinkle, burn. It follows a clear order: preparation (verses 1-9), three sacrifices in a logical progression (sin offering to deal with impurity, burnt offering of complete dedication, and ordination offering shared as a meal, verses 10-34), the seven-day duration and the altar's consecration (verses 35-37), the daily offering (verses 38-42), and a closing divine speech (verses 42-46). That speech shifts from instruction to promise, with God as the subject of every verb: I will meet, I will consecrate, I will dwell, and I am the LORD their God. The final line repeats the formula that runs through the plague narrative, that people “will know that I am the LORD”, now applied not to judgment but to God's presence among his people.

outline.t: The bull of the sin offering
The first ram: a burnt offering
The ram of ordination and the priests' portion
Succession, the ordination meal, and seven days of atonement
The daily offering and God's promise to dwell among Israel

doctrines.note: The word for making atonement (kipper) appears repeatedly here, for the priests and even for the altar. Before anyone can mediate for others, they themselves need atonement, and the place of worship must be purified. Atonement in this chapter is God's provided means of making the unholy fit to approach him.

Verse 45, “I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God”, echoes the covenant promise that runs from Genesis 17:7 to Revelation 21:3. The priesthood and the altar exist to serve that relationship.

Holiness spreads from God to what he claims: priests, garments, and altar are consecrated, and the altar becomes “most holy”. Only what God sets apart can stand in his presence, and the ceremony shows that this setting apart is his gift.

words.note: Kipper, to make atonement. Its exact root sense is debated: some link it to covering, others to wiping clean or to paying a ransom. In the priestly texts it describes the removal of sin and impurity so that people and places can be in God's presence. The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) takes its name from this word.

Millu, filling or setting, used here for ordination (the ram of ordination is literally the ram of filling). The idiom comes from the phrase to fill the hand, meaning to install someone in office. Elsewhere in Exodus the same word describes gemstones for mounting in a setting (25:7).

Mashach, to anoint, to pour or smear oil on someone or something to set it apart. From this verb comes mashiach, anointed one, the word behind Messiah (and, through Greek, Christ). Priests, kings, and objects in the sanctuary were anointed.

Olah, burnt offering, from the verb to go up, since the whole animal went up in smoke to God. It was the one sacrifice burned entirely on the altar, a gift of complete dedication, and it forms the regular morning and evening offering of verses 38-42.

christ: The letter to the Hebrews reads this chapter's system of priests and daily offerings as a pattern that Christ fulfills and completes. It contrasts the priests who stand day after day offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins, with Christ, who “offered for all time one sacrifice for sins” and sat down at the right hand of God (Hebrews 10:11-12). Aaron needed atonement before he could serve; Christ, Hebrews says, did not need to offer sacrifices first for his own sins (Hebrews 7:27). The anointing of the priests anticipates the title Christ, the Anointed One, and the promise of verse 45 comes to its fulfillment when John says that the Word “made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14) and when Revelation announces that God's dwelling is with humanity (Revelation 21:3). Paul says Christ gave himself as a fragrant offering to God (Ephesians 5:2), using the language of the pleasing aroma found in this chapter. These are the New Testament's own readings, drawn as fulfillment of a pattern rather than as hidden meanings in the ceremony's details.

hard.q: Why did God require animal sacrifice, and how should Christians read these rituals now?
hard.a:
Animal sacrifice can seem strange or troubling to modern readers. In the ancient world it was a universal language of worship, and the Old Testament takes that language and fills it with Israel's understanding of God. Sacrifices here are not food for a hungry god (Psalm 50:12-13 mocks that idea), and they are not bribes. They are God's provided means of cleansing, dedication, and fellowship, and they teach that sin is serious, that it costs life, and that God himself provides the way back. The prophets insisted that sacrifice without justice and a changed heart was worthless (Isaiah 1:11-17; Hosea 6:6), which shows that the rituals were never meant as mechanical transactions.

Christians read these chapters in light of Christ. Most traditions hold that the sacrificial system has been fulfilled and ended by his death, as Hebrews argues, so that the ceremonies are no longer practiced but still teach about sin, holiness, and grace. Jewish tradition, after the temple's destruction in AD 70, came to emphasize prayer, study of the Torah, and deeds of kindness in place of sacrifice. Readers in both traditions find in these chapters an account of what it means for a holy God to live among people.

questions: The priests had to be washed and atoned for before they could serve others. How does receiving grace yourself shape how you serve others?
The blood on ear, hand, and foot suggests that the whole person is set apart for God. Which part of your life do you most often keep for yourself?
The chapter says the whole purpose of the exodus was that God might dwell among his people. How does that change what you think salvation is for?
